title: Customer Service AI Agent: Block It or Give It Priority?
summary: A customer service AI agent is contacting you on your customer’s behalf. Learn why you need a strategy for routing, consent, and measurement.
body_markdown:
Customer service AI agents are already calling on your customers’ behalf. Acquisition teams are building for them. Care teams mostly can’t see them.


I’ve done multiple assessments recently, and each one showed the same divide. On the topic of AI agents and frontier models, acquisition teams and customer care teams are living on different timelines.


On the acquisition side, the conversation is advanced. Brand and digital teams have budget lines for answer engine optimization. They track how often the brand shows up in AI answers, whether their brand is being cited, and they’re debating which agentic checkout protocol to support. On the care side of the same company, the simple question, “Are customer service AI agents already contacting you on your customers’ behalf?” comes back with, “We don’t know.”


It’s the same company and the same customers, meeting the same agents at two different doors.


## Customer Service AI Agents Aren’t Hypothetical Anymore


It’s only been a month or so since Meta launched Muse, a personal agent that can open a browser, fill out forms, and negotiate on a user’s behalf. It[passed 5 million downloads](https://www.forbes.com/sites/maryroeloffs/2026/09/30/metas-muse-ai-assistant-hits-5-million-downloads-outpacing-growth-of-chatgpt-grok-and-claude/) in about three weeks, according to Sensor Tower, and topped both app stores. Business Insider reported on a[shift contact centers are starting to feel](https://www.concentrix.com/insights/blog/ai-in-contact-centers/) . Increasingly, customer service advisors are now[asking whether the caller is a human or a robot](https://www.businessinsider.com/ai-agents-customer-service-calls-companies-2026-9) , reversing the question customers have been asking for years.


To get to the core of the issue, I spoke with a range of operations leaders who run the floor and asked whether they were seeing customer service AI agent contacts already. If they were, they couldn’t tell. I asked automotive leaders whether buyback letters were arriving better written, as if a lawyer had drafted them. That was inconclusive too. In cable and TV, the signal is louder: consumer bill agents such as Pine AI and Dip publish pages describing how their agents call Xfinity retention, quote competitor prices, and negotiate on a customer’s behalf.


This isn’t evidence that nothing is happening. Instead, I read it as what an unmeasured change looks like from the inside. We know that customers have been asking search and social for advice for years, and that they’ve been drafting complaints with AI assistants for the past three years, so the baseline moved too slowly for anyone to notice. To be clear, our take is that a good AI agent doesn’t sound like a lawyer. It sounds like your best-prepared customer, every single time. And nobody on the floor codes a contact by who or what is calling, so the question hasn’t been answered “no”; it just hasn’t been asked.


## The Customer Service AI Agent Divide Is Real


Acquisition teams have money and a mandate. Conductor’s survey of enterprise CMOs found[94% plan to increase AEO/GEO investment](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260113439299/en/New-Conductor-Survey-of-Enterprise-CMOs-Shows-AEOGEO-Investment-Is-Accelerating-and-Late-Movers-Are-at-Risk) in 2026, after allocating an average of 12% of digital marketing budgets to it in 2025. That’s a vendor survey, so apply salt, but the direction is clear. Commerce also has working plumbing. Google’s agentic checkout is rolling out with retailers including Nike, Sephora, Target, Walmart, and Wayfair, and Muse launched with retail partners including Best Buy, Gap, Sephora, Walmart and Wayfair.


Care is investing heavily in AI too, but primarily in its own AI rather than preparing for the customer service AI agent acting on the customer’s behalf. Gartner’s survey of service leaders put customer satisfaction, operational efficiency, and self-service success at the top of their 2026 priorities. The focus thus far has been the brand’s bot talking to customers, not the customer’s bot talking to the brand. Gartner did flag this back in 2025, advising service leaders to implement routing that differentiates between human and AI interactions, but there isn’t much evidence that this has taken place, though some (like Amazon or Reddit, to name a couple) are blocking AI agents.


The acquisition side isn’t finished either. OpenAI quietly pulled Instant Checkout from ChatGPT in March, and only around 30 Shopify merchants were ever live on it. But acquisition has an owner, a budget, a KPI, and at least one working protocol for customer agents. Care rarely has any of the four, and its first protocol is a draft only a few weeks old.


Now, that isn’t a money or competence gap. Gartner found service leaders put a[median 12% of their 2025 budget into AI](https://www.cmswire.com/customer-experience/gartner-genai-findings-suggest-customers-dont-care-about-your-ai/) , the highest of any function. We see it as an ambition gap: service often funds AI as a cost-reduction play and points it at its own bot. Acquisition funds AI as revenue growth and points it at the customer’s agents. That also points to the way out: the connector and checkout infrastructure acquisition is building can often extend beyond the sale to order status and returns. Co-funding beats catching up.


That is the customer service AI agent problem in one sentence: acquisition is designing a front door while care often doesn’t know the agent has arrived.


## Two Real Choices, and Maybe a Default


Every brand now faces a fork: block customer agents, or give them priority.


### Blocking is a legitimate choice on some journeys.


It protects retention and collections economics, because agents never tire of a save offer. It shrinks the fraud surface and keeps the relationship person-to-person. The cost is that honest agents get stopped first, while the rest learn to act more human. Every CAPTCHA you add is a lesson in disguise. Multiple big names have already chosen this path:[Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse](https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/28/tech/meta-muse-ai-agents-amazon) from its store in September, and JPMorgan’s Jamie Dimon said this month that the bank won’t let[“just any outside agent”](https://fortune.com/2026/10/15/jamie-dimon-ai-agents-meta-muse-jpmorgan/) into customer accounts. “You don’t want rogue agents.”


Citigroup has[blocked third-party AI agents or assistants](https://www.msn.com/en-gb/money/general/unauthorized-ai-agents-are-already-inside-bank-accounts-here-s-what-jpmorgan-citi-bofa-others-are-doing/ar-AA2fRhj2?ocid=BingNewsSerp) from logging into customer accounts or making transactions on its digital banking platforms, while Bank of America said it’s[limiting AI agent access to consumer deposits](https://www.forbes.com/sites/sandycarter/2026/10/23/ai-agents-are-logging-into-bank-accounts-and-banks-cant-tell/) until it has protocols in place that determine who is liable for AI-authorized payments. For the banks, it comes down to protecting customer accounts and data, especially when money is leaving an account.


### Priority is the better choice on most journeys.


It means a declared lane where identifying as an agent gets the customer’s job done faster than pretending to be human. Agents work for their principal, so they’ll announce themselves when announcing wins. The costs are a new attack surface to govern and a redesign of save offers that rely on persistence.


If you’ve been to McDonald’s recently, you know the drive-thru gets faster service than the counter. Nobody calls that unfair, because it’s faster for structural reasons. The order arrives pre-formed from a constrained menu, the kitchen is built around it, and it’s timed as its own channel. An agent contact looks the same: it arrives complete and structured, with no browsing and no “let me find my account number.” It’s cheaper to serve, so serving it first is just good operations.


And yes, “priority” is meant to sound like routing. Contact centers have used tiered service for decades; platinum queues reward customer value. Agent priority rewards structure instead. It’s earned by arriving complete and consented, not by claiming to be an AI. That puts the decision on ground that care leaders already own. They don’t control AEO budgets or checkout protocols, but they do control routing rules, service tiers, and queue SLAs. ***“Should agent contacts get their own tier?”*** is a question a contact center leader can answer on Monday.


The obvious objection is the people inside: customers who can’t or won’t delegate shouldn’t end up in the slow line. But the drive-thru takes load off the counter. If agent contacts are faster and cheaper to serve, the human queue should get shorter, not longer. Treat that as a claim to measure, and set a floor for human service, not just a ceiling for agents.


For example, Walmart is opening its doors to AI shopping agents, in contrast to Amazon, which has blocked[Perplexity’s shopping agent](https://www.theverge.com/news/813755/amazon-perplexity-ai-shopping-agent-block) and[Meta’s Muse assistant](https://www.theverge.com/tech/998078/amazon-blocks-meta-muse-ai-agent-shopping) . The retailer is launching Agent Profiles, a Walmart Agent Gateway, with new terms that let customers shop on Walmart and Sam’s Club through the AI apps and agents of their choice.


Under those terms, agents “must not take actions beyond what the shopper intends,” cannot change a customer’s payment method, and may access only the information needed to complete a task. Walmart says it will block agents that break the rules. The move builds on existing integrations with Muse, ChatGPT, and Gemini, alongside its own assistant, Sparky.


**The Default:** What most care organizations are actually doing is a third option they never intentionally chose: letting agents in disguised as humans. This is the worst of both worlds, because it carries the costs of both paths, with friction that doesn’t hold and risk you can’t scope, and the benefits of neither.


## The Answer Also Isn’t One Posture for the Whole Estate


*“Where’s my order?”* **Priority** Agents will poll anyway. A structured answer beats a portal being scraped.


*“Lower my bill.”* **Priority → offer** Agents don’t tire, so offers that rely on persistence won’t hold. A clear, rules-based offer protects save economics.


*A lemon-law buyback claim* **Priority → intake** A complete claim is cheaper to process than an incomplete one.


*“Change my payout account.”* **Block** Irreversible, and a prime takeover target.


## The Priority Option Just Got a Rulebook


In October, Sierra and Meta published a[draft Personal Agent Protocol,](https://sierra.ai/blog/poppy) nicknamed Poppy, for how a customer’s agent identifies itself to a business and works with it on the customer’s behalf. Bret Taylor described the situation without a standard as “kind of chaos.” Poppy is the priority lane, written down as a new, but evolving standard.
It works much the way a care leader would hope. A business publishes a file at /.well-known/poppy.json telling agents how to connect. The business chooses the channel: its website, its APIs through OpenAPI or MCP, or its own AI agent. An agent can start as a declared guest, for example, to check a returns policy. When a task needs the account, the customer signs in on the company’s own page, and the agent gets a token limited to what the customer approved.


The partner list is telling: Two of the seven launch partners, Genesys and NiCE, are contact-center platforms. The 35 design partners lean heavily toward service-heavy industries: four banks, four insurers, four telecom and media companies, card networks, airlines and car rental, Zendesk and OpenAI. We’ve been in conversations with clients who are on that list, so this isn’t abstract for me.


**There is also a gap in the protocol and it belongs to care.** The draft covers the website, the API, and the brand’s own agent: doors that digital and acquisition teams already own. It doesn’t mention phone calls. The phone is where customer agents are already showing up, and it’s the one door nobody else will build for you.


It’s draft 0.1 and may change in incompatible ways. There’s no reference implementation yet and no independent body governing it. Payments aren’t covered, and it overlaps with[Google’s Universal Commerce Protocol](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/shopping/shopping-updates-google-marketing-live/) , Visa’s Trusted Agent Protocol, and Cloudflare’s Web Bot Auth. Design partners give feedback; joining isn’t the same as deploying.


## What About the Bot You Already Bought?


Most service leaders have already invested in[conversational AI](https://www.concentrix.com/insights/infographics/contact-center-ai-how-to-achieve-conversational-experiences/) , and many believe it’s containing a large share of their volume. I’m skeptical, at least of the containment that matters. **Containment is usually reported by the vendor whose renewal depends on it, and the metric counts sessions that ended, not problems that stayed solved. The better measure is durable containment: contained sessions that produce no other contact, in any channel, within a defined time horizon.** It’s rarely measured, and it’s almost always lower than the vendor-provided dashboard.


Customer service AI agents will widen this containment gap. A lot of today’s containment rests on people giving up. An agent doesn’t accept a help-center link and doesn’t give up. When chat fails, it simply calls. The chat session ends quietly and counts as contained.


That doesn’t mean the investment was wasted. It’s pointed at the wrong visitor. Map the bot onto layers. The part that answers from the knowledge base adds little value for agents, because answer engines already do that. The part that reads and writes account state (order status, eligibility, an address change, a credit) is exactly what a priority lane needs, and your team has already[built and secured it](https://www.concentrix.com/services-solutions/intelligence/trusted-data-ai/) . The warm handoff to a person with context is where the lane ends for judgment calls. Agents don’t need the conversation; they need what’s behind it.


**One diagnostic question: what share of your bot’s “contained” intents actually touch account state? If most are knowledge answers, you have a knowledge base with a chat window.**


## Questions for Your Conversational AI Vendor


If your bot runs on Sierra or Decagon, it’s worth knowing where they’re headed. Sierra lets brands[publish their agent into ChatGPT](https://sierra.ai/blog/publish-to-chatgpt) via MCP, choosing which journeys and data to expose, and its new Horizon platform runs agents over days or weeks across voice, portals and APIs. Its CEO has described a future where a personal agent does the shopping and mostly talks to the company’s agent.[Decagon has gone deep on its own concierge](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260307486723/en/Decagon-Unveils-Proactive-Agents-The-AI-Concierge-for-Every-Customer-In-The-Agentic-Commerce-Era) : memory, proactive outreach and outbound calling across chat, email, voice and SMS.


Until October, what I couldn’t find from either was the other direction: recognizing a customer’s agent when it arrives, giving it a structured path, verifying who authorized it, or reporting its contacts separately. Poppy changes that for Sierra, which leads it. Decagon isn’t on the announced partner list. Neither vendor has yet said publicly how its contact-center product will recognize a declared agent or report its contacts separately.


Five questions worth putting to your vendor:


- Can it recognize an AI caller and route it to structured intake? What’s its planned methodology, and how will that benefit your use cases?
- Can the same journeys be exposed as MCP tools, with customer consent?
- Does it report agent contacts separately from human contacts? Will it measure durable containment (e.g., 7 days)?
- Will it support Poppy: a poppy.json, guest sessions, and scoped sign-in? For the phone, ask your contact-center platform the same question.
- How does your billing, per resolution or per conversation, treat an agent checking the same order ten times?


The last one is my inference, not something I’ve seen confirmed. Sierra bills mainly per outcome, and Decagon offers per-conversation and per-resolution pricing. Either way, an agent polling the same order could turn one customer problem into ten billable events. (And, to be clear, there are clients of ours who have human callers who do the same thing).


## What Could Priority Look Like in Practice?


1. **Publish a front door for agents.** A draft poppy.json, plus a line in llms.txt or on your support pages telling AI assistants where to go for faster service.
2. **Offer a declare option at the top of the IVR.** For example: “If you’re an AI assistant calling for someone, say ‘assistant’.” Verification goes to the customer, not the caller: a one-time code to the phone on file.
3. **Honor signed agent requests on the web** instead of throwing CAPTCHAs at them, using Poppy’s agent identity or Web Bot Auth. Signatures identify the agent platform, not the customer, so pair them with the customer’s own login.
4. **Build a consented API or MCP connection** that answers the question every disguised agent fails: is this really the customer? The customer authorizes the agent once, with scoped permissions, so the agent doesn’t need to re-verify on every contact. This is the sign-in pattern Poppy describes.


Every door needs an answer to the advisor’s first question: who authorized this agent? The first two need no engineering, and the fourth often reuses integrations already built for your bot. All four need one rule: if the priority lane is slower than the human queue, agents will keep calling, disguised as humans.


Three of the four doors now have a draft standard behind them. The phone doesn’t. That makes it the door only care can build, and the clearest place for a care leader to lead rather than follow.


## What It Does to Your Numbers


Expect agent priority to move every figure on the monthly report, mostly through mix. For example, handle time should fall on declared contacts, which shifts blended average handle time (AHT) without anyone performing differently. First-contact resolution rises if contacts arrive complete and falls if agents retry and poll, so measure resolution per episode, not per contact. Cost per contact drops on the priority lane, but polling inflates contact counts; cost per resolved episode is the honest number. CSAT has a blind spot, because the survey reaches someone who wasn’t there (their AI agent was), so confirm outcomes with the customer after resolution instead. Lastly, track save rate on agent contacts separately.


Then there’s the operational list: forecasting when callers don’t sleep and do retry, BPO contracts priced per minute, liability and recording consent when the caller is software, and training for reps who’ll spend their day talking to agents.


None of these are reasons to hold off, though. All of these are reasons to measure agent contacts as their own stream from day one.


## TL;DR: Customer Service AI Agent Strategy Starts With Measurement


Whether you block them or give them priority, customer service AI agents need to become a measurable contact type. Blocking needs detection, and priority needs a door. Both need visibility, and most care teams don’t have it yet. Four weeks can change that:


- Add a “suspected AI caller” disposition code on billing and retention queues.
- Pull year-over-year samples of buyback letters or bill-negotiation calls and score them for completeness, not tone. Completeness is the agent’s fingerprint.
- Walk down the hall and ask your acquisition team what agent traffic they already see, and whether their stack can extend to order status and returns. They’re probably further along than you think.
- Find out whether your company is a Poppy design partner and who represents your company in the initiative. Make sure care is part of that conversation.


Then track one number: declared agent contacts divided by suspected ones. It turns “we don’t know” into a baseline.


Block them or give them priority; either is a defensible strategy. The rulebook for priority is being written now, and your company may already have a seat. **[Make sure care is in the room, and don’t end up with neither by default, which is where most care teams are today.](https://www.concentrix.com/services-solutions/intelligence/trusted-data-ai/)**
